nameStory: The name "felwort" comes from an old Germanic word meaning "field plant," though this particular species prefers wetlands rather than fields. The "marsh" part of the name accurately reflects where you'll actually find this delicate member of the gentian family - in boggy, wet areas across northern regions.
description: Marsh felwort is a small, delicate annual wildflower that grows just 2-8 inches tall. It produces tiny white or pale blue four-petaled flowers that seem almost star-like when fully open. The plant has a simple, branching structure with narrow, opposite leaves that clasp the stem. Despite being in the gentian family, it's much smaller and more inconspicuous than its showy cousins like bottle gentian.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny four-petaled flowers, usually white or very pale blue, about 1/4 inch across with a delicate, star-like appearance when fully open. Each petal has fine parallel veins that catch the light.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged in opposite pairs that clasp the stem without stalks. They feel thin and smooth between your fingers, almost papery when dry.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that rarely exceeds 8 inches tall, with a branching pattern that creates a small, delicate spray of stems from the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small oval capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The capsules are about the size of a grain of rice and feel firm when ripe.

habitat: Found in calcareous (limestone-rich) wetlands, including fens, wet meadows, and marshy shores of northern lakes and ponds. In New England, it's extremely rare and typically found in specialized alkaline bog habitats, often growing alongside sedges, wild mint, and other moisture-loving plants. It prefers areas with consistent moisture and cool temperatures.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves in late spring, easily overlooked among other wetland vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from July through August, producing their tiny star-like blossoms that open fully in bright sunlight but may close on cloudy days.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen in late summer to early fall, then the entire plant dies back as it completes its annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence - seeds lie dormant in the wet soil until the following spring.

funFact: Marsh felwort is so rare in New England that it's been documented only six times across the entire region - you're more likely to spot a moose than find one of these tiny wildflowers!
confusionNotes: The tiny four-petaled white flowers might be confused with small chickweeds or pearlworts, but those have five petals and different leaf arrangements. Remember: four petals plus opposite leaves in a wetland setting points to marsh felwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its rarity, marsh felwort has a circumpolar distribution, meaning the same species grows across northern regions of North America, Europe, and Asia - making any New England sighting a special connection to the global Arctic flora.
compareHints: As the only Lomatogonium species in New England, marsh felwort differs from other gentian family members by its tiny size and four-petaled flowers. Most gentians have five petals and are much larger, while marsh felwort's delicate four-petaled blooms and diminutive stature make it unique among its relatives.
